panels.title: From records to causal estimates
panels.sentence: B adjusts for why each patient received their drug instead of only learning from the records as A does: compared with A, its regret is 16% lower (not a clear difference), the average effect has 88% smaller bias, and it gives numbers for 12.8% of the patient-option pairs where similar patients are too few instead of 100.0%; its error on each patient's effect (PEHE) shows no clear improvement on 3 of 3 comparisons. The naive comparison of group averages has a regret of 0.0633 (A 0.0126, B 0.0106) and its interval contains the true SGLT2i vs DPP-4i effect for 13.9% of patients (B 94.4%).

panels.note: Mean over 20 synthetic cohorts with its 95% interval. The naive comparison uses the plain average HbA1c change in each drug group of the records for every patient. C and D do not change B's estimate, so they are not repeated here.

panels.title: What C adds
panels.sentence: C splits B's estimate into one contribution per patient detail that adds up to the estimate (largest error 2.7e-16) and shows only the details whose 95% interval excludes zero; 11% to 18% of the drivers it shows are not true effect modifiers, and A's top features match the true modifiers more often than C's on 2 of 3 comparisons.

panels.note: Drivers describe the estimate, never a cause. A's SHAP explains a prediction model, not an effect. An interval past 100% is the t-interval of the 20 cohorts as the ablation wrote it (most cohorts score 100%), not a value above 100%.

panels.title: What D adds
panels.sentence: D finds cited passages and writes the explanation, and checks every draft before it is shown: on the 60 gold questions 100% of the quoted sentences were supported by their cited passage and 0 answers contained dose text; the local model's drafts failed a check on 75% of the 20 golden questions, so the template answered instead.
